system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
[person] was admitted on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021 after a stay of 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours in the ward. The main problem was a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) linked to a Schilley catheter (a tube for dialysis) in the right femoral vein (large vein in the thigh). This led to bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart valve), specifically with vegetation (clot of bacteria) on the mitral valve, as seen on an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) on 11/18. There was also pyogenic spondylodiscitis (infection of the spine and discs) at the L3/L4 level, causing low back pain and gait disturbance (difficulty walking). A CT scan (X-ray scan) of the lumbosacral spine on 11/12 showed a fracture due to bone fragility at L1, gas in the spinal canal at L2/L3 possibly from a disc herniation (disc slipping out), and possible infection. An MRI (magnetic scan) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection near the spine). Additionally, an MRI on 25/10/2020 showed a left ileopsoas abscess (pus pocket in the hip muscle) measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm.

[person] came in with severe left lower back pain, weakness, and altered gait, but no fever, nausea, or vomiting. The catheter dressing was leaking. During the stay, the infection was identified as Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of resistant bacteria). The catheter was removed on 11/08, and antibiotic therapy with Vancomycin (an antibiotic) was started. An attempt to drain the psoas abscess percutaneously (through the skin) on 12/02 was not done because bowel loops (intestines) were in the way. Imaging showed improvement in the spine infections, so conservative treatment (non-surgical care) was continued. [person] remained afebrile (no fever) with negative blood cultures. Due to immobility, a sacral pressure injury (bed sore on the tailbone) developed, which was treated with surgical debridement (cleaning of dead tissue) and local care. [person] requires hemodialysis (machine filtering waste from blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays using an arteriovenous fistula (surgical connection for dialysis) in the left arm, though a local stenosis (narrowing) was noted.

On examination, [person] is in good general condition, pale, hydrated, and breathing normally on room air. He is conscious and oriented. Breath sounds are clear with slight crackles at the bases. Heart rhythm is irregular but sounds are normal with no murmurs. The abdomen is soft and painless. Limbs are warm and well-perfused (good blood flow). The left arm fistula has a thrill (vibration from blood flow). There is slight swelling and skin changes on the lower legs. Cultures showed Vancomycin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus initially, followed by Citrobacter koseri and Staphylococcus capitis, with negative cultures from 11/28 onwards.

For discharge, [person] must take 0.5 g of Vancomycin after each hemodialysis session until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after the last negative blood culture. A phlebography (X-ray of veins) of the fistula is needed to check the narrowing site, possibly with ultrasound first. [person] is on the list for this, and [organization] will contact you to schedule it. [person] has an outpatient follow-up on 16/01/2021 for pressure injury reassessment, with home care instructions provided. A cardiology follow-up for amyloidosis (a condition affecting heart tissue) was missed on 09/09 and is rescheduled for 01/13. Motor rehabilitation is scheduled for 01/13, and we are awaiting an appointment from the physiatry department at [organization] requested on 12/27. Please check the pelvic MRI report from 12/16. Previous chronic medications should be continued. Dialysis is on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. The amyloidosis clinic is on 01/13, and the pressure injury surgery clinic is on 01/16. Transportation for dialysis is by stretcher taxi {omitted}.
